Glossary

    Space: lines, planes, solids

    Words: 2557

    Plane geometry plus one more dimension. Almost every task of solid geometry is solved by finding a flat figure in the solid: a cross-section, a net, a right triangle inside.

    Main idea of the page #

    Space does not demand new laws as much as it seems: distances in it are Pythagoras' theorem (applied twice), lateral surfaces are areas of the rectangles and triangles of a net, volumes are «base area times height», with a factor of one third for pointed solids. Only one thing is new: volume grows as the cube of a linear size. The block closes geometry; the coordinate view of space is in block 12.

    Step 0 · Hook

    1 · The edge doubled, so the volume doubled? #

    A cube with edge 1 has volume 1. The edge was doubled. «The volume doubled»? A cube with edge 2 is made of eight unit cubes: two layers of four. The volume grew 8 times. The area of each face grew 4 times. The same rule as in block 11, but with a third dimension.

    Figure 65. Twice the edge - 2³ = 8 times the volume.

    Step 1 · Concept

    2 · Lines, planes, solids #

    • Two lines in space can meet, be parallel or be Skew linesLines that do not meet and do not lie in one plane.To the glossary : not meet and not lie in one plane.
    • A line is perpendicular to a plane if it is perpendicular to two intersecting lines of that plane. Its segment from a point to the plane is the distance from the point to the plane.
    • A prism and a cylinder have two equal parallel bases; a pyramid and a cone have one base and an apex. The height is the perpendicular from the apex (or from the upper base) to the plane of the base. The ApothemThe height of a side face of a regular pyramid.To the glossary of a regular pyramid is the height of a side face.
    • The Lateral and total surfaceThe lateral surface is all the faces except the bases; the total one includes the bases.To the glossary is all the faces except the bases; the total one includes the bases.
    Step 2 · Law

    3 · Laws of space #

    Volume: a prism is S·h, a pyramid is a third

    Vprism=Vcylinder=Sbase·h,Vpyramid=Vcone=13Sbase·hV_{\text{prism}} = V_{\text{cylinder}} = S_{\text{base}} \cdot h,\qquad V_{\text{pyramid}} = V_{\text{cone}} = \frac{1}{3} S_{\text{base}} \cdot h
    Vball=43πR3,Ssphere=4πR2V_{\text{ball}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3,\qquad S_{\text{sphere}} = 4\pi R^2

    The lateral surface is the perimeter of the base times the height

    Slat. prism=Pbase·h,Slat. cylinder=2πRhS_{\text{lat. prism}} = P_{\text{base}} \cdot h,\qquad S_{\text{lat. cylinder}} = 2\pi R h

    for a right prism and a right cylinder.

    Corollary of the law «The lateral surface is the perimeter of the base times the height»

    Solids of revolution

    lcylinder=h,lcone2=R2+h2l_{\text{cylinder}} = h,\qquad l_{\text{cone}}^2 = R^2 + h^2

    A cylinder is formed by rotating a rectangle about a side, a cone by rotating a right triangle about a leg, a ball by rotating a disc about a diameter. The axial section of a cylinder is a rectangle 2R × h, of a cone an isosceles triangle with base 2R. The Slant heightThe segment that sweeps out the lateral surface of a cylinder or a cone as it rotates.To the glossary of a cylinder equals its height, the slant height of a cone l is found from l² = R² + h².

    Figure 66. Corollary: a cone is formed by rotating a right triangle about a leg; the hypotenuse becomes the slant height.

    Why it is so. The side about which the figure rotates becomes the axis of the solid, and the opposite side of the rectangle or the hypotenuse of the triangle sweeps out the lateral surface - that is the slant height. In the axial section of a cone the height, the radius of the base and the slant height form a right triangle, so Pythagoras' theorem works (block 11). The lateral surface of a cylinder unrolls into a rectangle 2πR × l, and with l = h this is the law of the lateral surface.

    Diagonal of a cuboid

    d2=a2+b2+c2d^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2

    Volumes of similar solids

    V1V2=k3\frac{V_1}{V_2} = k^3

    Tests for parallelism and perpendicularity in space

    A line is parallel to a plane if it is parallel to some line of that plane. Two planes are parallel if two intersecting lines of one of them are parallel to the other; through a point outside a plane there passes exactly one plane parallel to it. A line is perpendicular to a plane if it is perpendicular to two intersecting lines of that plane.

    Space is checked with a plane: to prove parallelism or perpendicularity, look for the right line in the plane itself, and there the laws of block 10 already work.

    Step 3 · Why it is so

    4 · Where the formulas come from #

    Base area times height. A prism can be pictured as a stack of thin equal «tiles» in the shape of the base; their number is proportional to the height.

    One third. A cube can be cut into three equal pyramids with their apex at one vertex of the cube, each standing on one of the three opposite faces. So a pyramid with the same base and height takes a third of the prism. The same holds for a cone and a cylinder.

    Lateral surface. The net of the lateral surface of a right prism is a rectangle with sides PbaseP_{\text{base}} and h; of a cylinder, a rectangle with sides 2πR2\pi R and h.

    Figure 67. The lateral surface of a right prism is a rectangle with sides P and h.

    Diagonal. Pythagoras twice: the diagonal of the base is a2+b2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, then it and the side edge c are the legs of a triangle with hypotenuse d.

    Figure 68. The diagonal of a cuboid: Pythagoras twice, d² = a² + b² + c².

    Step 4 · Limits

    5 · Where the laws break #

    The lateral and the total surface are different quantities. The total surface of a cylinder is 2πRh+2πR22\pi R h + 2\pi R^2: two bases are added.

    The height of a pyramid is neither the apothem nor a side edge. The volume takes the height, the lateral surface of a regular pyramid takes the apothem.

    Volume grows as the cube. Increasing all sizes k times increases the volume k3k^3 times and the surface area k2k^2 times.

    Step 5 · Practice

    6 · Tasks in the NMT format #

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    The dimensions of a cuboid are 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. Find its volume.

    Law: base area times height.

    2·3·4=242 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24. 52 is the total surface area, not the volume.

    Short answer · 2 points

    The side of the base of a regular square prism is 3 cm, the lateral surface area is 60 cm². Find the volume of the prism (in cm³).

    Laws: lateral surface and volume of a prism.

    The perimeter of the base is 12, so h=60:12=5h = 60 : 12 = 5. The base is a square of area 9; V=9·5=45V = 9 \cdot 5 = 45. A task of this type was among the hardest at NMT 2026: two laws in one task, and the first of them «hides» in the word «lateral».

    Short answer · 2 points

    The radius of the base of a cone is 3 cm, the height is 4 cm. Find the volume of the cone. Write the value of Vπ\frac{V}{\pi} as your answer.

    Law: volume of a cone.

    V=13π·9·4=12πV = \frac{1}{3}\pi \cdot 9 \cdot 4 = 12\pi. The slant height here is 5, but the volume takes the height.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Find the diagonal of a cube with edge 2.

    Law: diagonal of a cuboid.

    d=4+4+4=23d = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 4} = 2\sqrt{3}. 2√2 is the diagonal of a face, not of the cube.

    Short answer · 2 points

    How many edges of the cube ABCDA₁B₁C₁D₁ are parallel to the plane of the face ABCD?

    Law: test for a line parallel to a plane.

    The four edges of the upper face: each is parallel to an edge of the lower face that lies in the plane ABCD. The edges of the lower face lie in the plane itself, and the side edges cross it.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    ABCDA₁B₁C₁D₁ is a cuboid: ABCD is the lower base, AA₁, BB₁, CC₁, DD₁ are the side edges. Which of the lines is perpendicular to the plane ABCD?

    Figure 69. For the task: a cuboid and the plane of its lower base.

    Law: test for a line perpendicular to a plane.

    The edge CC₁ is perpendicular to two intersecting lines of the base, CB and CD, so by the test it is perpendicular to the plane ABCD. AB lies in the plane, B₁D₁ is parallel to it, AC₁ and A₁C are oblique.

    Short answer · 2 points

    The side of the base of a regular square pyramid is 6 cm, and the height is 4 cm. Find the volume of the pyramid (in cm³).

    Figure 70. For the task: a regular square pyramid and its height.

    Law: the volume of a pyramid is a third of the base area times the height.

    The base is a square: S = 6² = 36, V=13·36·4=48V = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 36 \cdot 4 = 48. Without the third you get 144, the volume of a prism.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Data on the figure · read and apply. The numbers for the solution are only on the figure: first write them down, then solve.

    Find the length of the diagonal AC₁ of the cuboid shown in the figure (in cm).

    Figure 71. For the task: a cuboid with labelled edges and its diagonal.

    Law: diagonal of a cuboid.

    From the figure: the edges are 12, 4 and 3. d=122+42+32=169=13d = \sqrt{12^2 + 4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Data on the figure · pick what is needed. The numbers are only on the figure, and among them is an extra one or a trap: the grid step, a scale that does not start at zero. Write down only what the solution needs.

    Find the volume of the cuboid shown in the figure (in cm³).

    Figure 72. For the task: a cuboid with three edges and the diagonal of the base labelled.

    Law: base area times height.

    The volume needs three edges: 5, 2 and 4. V = 5 · 2 · 4 = 40. The diagonal of the base √29 is not needed here. 76 is the total surface area, 11 is the sum of the three edges.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Data on the figure · read and connect. The numbers are only on the figure, and what you read goes into two laws: write the numbers down, then name both laws.

    Find the length of the vector BD₁ (see the figure).

    Figure 73. For the task: a cuboid on coordinate axes and the vector BD₁.

    Laws: coordinates of a vector (block 12) and the diagonal of a cuboid: the length of the vector BD₁ is that very diagonal.

    From the figure: AB = 6, AD = 2, AA₁ = 3, so B(6; 0; 0), D₁(0; 2; 3). The coordinates of a vector are end minus start: BD1→=(−6; 2; 3)\overrightarrow{BD_1} = (-6;\ 2;\ 3), the length is 36+4+9=7\sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = 7.
    Step 6 · Reverse move

    7 · Name the law yourself #

    Short answer · 2 points

    The edge of a cube was doubled. How many times did its volume increase?

    Law: volumes of similar solids.

    23=82^3 = 8.

    Short answer · 2 points

    The radius of a ball is 3 cm. Find the area of its surface. Write the value of Sπ\frac{S}{\pi} as your answer.

    Law: area of a sphere.

    4π·9=36π4\pi \cdot 9 = 36\pi. Curiously, at R = 3 the area of the sphere and the volume of the ball (43π·27=36π\frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot 27 = 36\pi) are numerically equal - but they are different quantities with different units.

    8 · Find the mistake in someone else's solution #

    Bohdan works out the paint for a cylindrical tank with a lid and a bottom: «The surface area is S=2πRhS = 2\pi R h».

    Where is the mistake?

    That is only the lateral surface. The bottom and the lid are two more discs: S=2πRh+2πR2S = 2\pi R h + 2\pi R^2 (the first limit).

    What you have after this page #

    Space comes down to the plane. Distances are Pythagoras twice, lateral surfaces are nets, volumes are base area times height and one third for pointed solids. Area grows as the square, volume as the cube.

    Frequency on this site, not in the NMT: this page has 12 trainer tasks, and they lean on these laws: Volume: a prism is S·h, a pyramid is a third - 6, Diagonal of a cuboid - 3, Tests for parallelism and perpendicularity in space - 2, Coordinates of a vector and the midpoint of a segment - 1, The lateral surface is the perimeter of the base times the height - 1, Volumes of similar solids - 1. In real NMT papers of 2024-2026 this block is needed in 14 tasks out of 132: The lateral surface is the perimeter of the base times the height - 8, Volume: a prism is S·h, a pyramid is a third - 5, Tests for parallelism and perpendicularity in space - 3, Diagonal of a cuboid - 1.

    You know this block if you:

    1. solve 8 tasks out of 10 on volumes and surfaces without a hint;
    2. can explain aloud where the one third in the volume of a pyramid comes from;
    3. find the mistake in someone else's solution, as in Bohdan's.
